claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution, and the components inside it inherit the package's version.

Pulumi packages come in two flavors, and each is versioned and released differently. Understanding the release artifact for each flavor is the foundation for the repository-layout advice in this guide.
The packaging-components page has anchors for 'source-based-plugin-packages' and 'executable-based-plugin-packages' sections.

Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow (apply a semver Git tag, then run `pulumi package publish`), typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
1. Apply a semver Git tag (for example, `v1.2.3`) to the repository.

1. Run [`pulumi package publish`](/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish/) to send the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and place the package in the Private Registry. This step often runs automated tests before publishing.
Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing source-based packages to the Private Registry.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
A repository containing multiple Pulumi packages must either release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that conflicts with how Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are supported and expected, with components shipping together at the package's version.

The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry (at pulumi.com/registry/packages/eks/) bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with the supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
A single `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it in the repository.
The example repository layout places `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repo root and components under a `components/` directory, defining a single package.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
In a package with ComponentA and ComponentB, releasing v1.0.0, then an enhancement to ComponentA yields v1.1.0, then a breaking change to ComponentB yields v2.0.0 under semver.
A 'Publishing packages' guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/publishing-packages/ covering publishing mechanics.

A thoughtful repository strategy is essential for managing Pulumi packages at scale. Group cohesive components into one package per repository so they version and release together; use separate repositories for unrelated component groups so each package can evolve at its own pace. stances.text: Pulumi recommends structuring Git repositories for publishing packages per the strategies described in this guide, and following them improves reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed of packages.
A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type; this is Pulumi's recommended practice.
Pulumi recommends defining exactly one package per repository, grouping a cohesive set of components inside that package, and using multiple repositories (one per package) for distinct packages.
Using a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components is technically possible but Pulumi does not recommend it.
